claims.text: The starting material is as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility.
Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C and strain rates of 10^-4–10^-2 s^-1.
Untreated HfNbTaTiZr has poor oxygen resistance that limits high-temperature use in air.
A thin Al2O3 coating will be deposited on the alloy by chemical vapor deposition.
The Al2O3 coating is stable at approximately 1000 °C.
CVD deposition will produce a conformal, thin ceramic interface layer.
The Al2O3 layer will adhere to as-cast HfNbTaTiZr during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
The Al2O3 coating will act as a barrier to oxygen diffusion into the bulk alloy.
Reduced oxygen diffusion will reduce oxidation and preserve the alloy's microstructural integrity.
The Al2O3 coating will be self-healing under thermal cycling.
Self-healing under thermal cycling will ensure continued oxidation protection.
Coated samples will have lower oxidation-induced weight gain than untreated samples after prolonged exposure near 1000 °C in air.
Coated samples will have less oxygen penetration than untreated samples after prolonged exposure near 1000 °C in air.
The coating will preserve room-temperature ductility at a level comparable to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr.
The coating will preserve high-temperature yield strength at a level comparable to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed operating boundary is approximately 1000 °C in an oxidizing atmosphere for tens to hundreds of hours, with mechanical testing at strain rates of 10^-4–10^-2 s^-1.
Long-term coating adhesion and thermal stresses during temperature cycling may indirectly impair mechanical performance.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes the coating as adherent and says self-healing ensures continued protection, while the uncertainty field acknowledges unresolved long-term adhesion and thermal-stress effects. The latter appropriately qualifies but also weakens the unqualified assurance of continued protection.
